subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: At the school water fountain Abhinav slipped and fell hard, and his tiffin skidded across the floor. About twenty children were in the corridor. Jaya stood with her water bottle, watching. Everyone else was watching too, and a few whispered. Somebody will go, Jaya thought. Somebody will tell Ma'am. Abhinav sat holding his knee. Nobody moved. A bell rang, and the crowd drifted off in twos and threes. Jaya walked to class with a tight throat, wondering how many of the others had thought exactly the same thing.

qa.q: About how many children were in the corridor when Abhinav fell?
qa.a: About twenty children were in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking while standing with the water bottle?
qa.a: Jaya assumed somebody else would go and tell Ma'am, so the sense of duty felt spread among everyone; afterwards the tight throat shows guilt and unease.

qa.q: What could Jaya do at that moment instead of waiting?
qa.a: Jaya could point at one person, or walk to the nearest teacher and say "Abhinav fell and needs help", since one clear step ends the waiting.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have experienced twenty children watching and nobody coming?
qa.a: Abhinav may have felt embarrassed and alone, holding a hurt knee while everyone watched but no one came near.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and does nothing because many others are watching too, each assuming someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: From the school bus window I saw it. Vandana fell off the swing and sat holding her elbow. About ten children formed a ring around her. Anirban was in it, twisting a shirt button. He looked at the girl next to him, who looked at the boy next to her. Everyone seemed to be waiting for somebody. After a full minute a girl at the back ran off toward the staff room, and the ring melted. I do not know what Anirban was thinking, but he was the last to leave, still looking back at Vandana.

qa.q: What was Anirban doing while standing in the ring?
qa.a: Anirban was twisting a shirt button.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling while looking at the girl next to him?
qa.a: Anirban may have been uneasy and unsure, waiting for someone else to move first; looking back at Vandana suggests some guilt, though the narrator cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Anirban have done in that first minute?
qa.a: Anirban could have pointed to one person and said "You, get Ma'am", or gone to the staff room himself, which breaks the waiting.

qa.q: What might Vandana have experienced during the minute when the ring of children stayed still?
qa.a: Vandana probably felt hurt, embarrassed and alone, sitting with a sore elbow while ten children watched without acting.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and waits for others to act, and a bystander's account shows each assuming someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
At recess in the village school at Chitrakoot, Anirban fell off the high swing and landed hard on the stones. He curled up, holding his arm.
A ring of children formed. Nikita stood at the front. She waited for someone to run for Masterji. Surely Pinku would, he was the class monitor. Pinku was looking at Rani. Rani was looking at Nikita.
Nobody moved. Anirban started to cry.
Then the peon, Ramdeen kaka, saw the crowd from the well, dropped his bucket, and ran over. He sent a girl for the teacher and knelt by Anirban.
Nikita walked back to class slowly. So many of us, she thought. And I just stood there.

qa.q: Who ran over from the well?
qa.a: The peon, Ramdeen kaka, ran over from the well.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she walked back to class?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed that she just stood there while so many watched.

qa.q: What could Nikita do next time a classmate gets hurt?
qa.a: She could run straight for a teacher herself, or point at one person and say, "You, go get Masterji," instead of waiting.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt lying on the stones with a crowd around him?
qa.a: He was probably in pain and frightened, and it may have felt lonely that so many watched and nobody helped at first.

grounding: Shows a child who does nothing when a classmate falls because many are watching and each assumes someone else will act.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
At the lockers in their Manchester school, two older girls knocked Soo-ah's books out of her arms and laughed. “Pick them up, then.”
Bilal saw it from three lockers down. So did about ten others. He waited. Someone will say something, he thought. Ms Hughes is just round the corner. Somebody will get her.
A boy near the stairs looked at Bilal. Bilal looked at the floor.
Soo-ah knelt and gathered her books alone. The older girls walked off.
At the bell, a lunch supervisor came by, saw Soo-ah's face and walked her to the head of year's office. Bilal went to maths. He couldn't stop thinking that there had been ten of them and one of her.

qa.q: How many others saw what happened at the lockers?
qa.a: About ten others saw it.

qa.q: What was Bilal thinking while he waited?
qa.a: He felt uneasy but assumed someone else would speak or get Ms Hughes, so he did nothing; later he felt guilty.

qa.q: What small step could Bilal have taken?
qa.a: He could have walked round the corner to fetch Ms Hughes himself, or simply helped Soo-ah pick up her books.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah have felt gathering her books alone?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and very alone, seeing so many people watch and nobody help.

grounding: Shows a child who does nothing while a classmate is bullied because many are watching and each expects someone else to act.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
At the district swimming club's Sunday session, Sachin slipped on the wet tiles near the diving board and hit his head. He sat up, dazed, holding it.
Twenty boys were around the pool. Manoj was nearest. He looked at the lifeguard's chair. Empty. He looked at the others. They were all looking too.
Somebody will call Coach, Manoj thought. Someone older.
Nobody did. Sachin tried to stand and wobbled.
Then Coach Iqbal came out of the office, saw him, and ran. He sat Sachin down, pressed a towel to his head and phoned his parents.
In the changing room, nobody spoke. Manoj stared at his locker, thinking he had been two steps away.

qa.q: Where did Sachin slip?
qa.a: He slipped on the wet tiles near the diving board.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel in the changing room?
qa.a: He felt guilty and quiet, thinking he had been two steps away and done nothing.

qa.q: What would you advise Manoj if it happens again?
qa.a: Go to the person yourself and shout for an adult by name, like "Coach Iqbal!", rather than waiting for someone older.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when nobody came at first?
qa.a: He was probably dazed and scared, and confused that so many boys stood around without helping.

grounding: Shows a child who doesn't help an injured boy because many others are watching and each assumes someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monday: At the school gate, a bigger boy snatched Gopika's cap and threw it onto the bus roof. Twenty kids stood there. Tarun looked around. Someone will tell, he thought. Nobody did. Gopika climbed into the bus with her head down.
Wednesday: In the canteen queue, Tarun heard two classmates. "I thought you'd say something." "I thought you would." His ears went hot. He had thought the same.
Friday: When the same boy grabbed Gopika's bag at the gate, Tarun didn't look around. He ran to Mr Iyer, on gate duty. "Sir, he's taking Gopika's bag. He did it Monday too." Mr Iyer went over at once, stood beside Gopika, got the bag back and took the boy to the office. Gopika gave Tarun a small nod.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy do with Gopika's cap on Monday?
qa.a: He threw it onto the bus roof.

qa.q: How was Tarun feeling when he heard the two classmates in the canteen queue?
qa.a: Tarun felt ashamed, his ears going hot, because he had also waited for someone else to act.

qa.q: What made Tarun's choice on Friday work?
qa.a: He stopped waiting for the crowd and went straight to one adult on duty, saying clearly what was happening and that it had happened before.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Gopika?
qa.a: With twenty kids watching and nobody helping, Gopika probably felt alone and embarrassed as she got on the bus with her head down.

grounding: Shows a child who first does nothing while many others watch a classmate being picked on, each assuming someone else will act, and later acts.
